questions.question: A 6-character code uses the digits 0-9 with no digit repeated. Which count is correct, and why?
options: 10 · 9 · 8 · 7 · 6 · 5, because each step always has one fewer option, whatever was chosen
10⁶, because each slot can hold any of the 10 digits
6¹⁰, because there are 6 slots and 10 digits
C(10, 6), because we are choosing 6 digits
questions.explanation: The generalized product rule applies: which digits remain depends on earlier picks, but how many remain (10, 9, 8, ...) does not. C(10, 6) would ignore the order of the digits.

questions.question: Why are there (n − 1)! ways to seat n knights at a round table when rotations count as the same?
options: Because one knight must always sit in seat 1, so we lose one factor of n
Because the map from n! line-ups to tables is n-to-1: each table comes from one line-up per starting knight
Because there are n − 1 gaps between n knights
Because a round table has no first seat, so we subtract 1 from n before taking the factorial
questions.explanation: Each circular seating is produced by exactly n permutations (choose who you list first). The division rule gives n!/n = (n − 1)!.

questions.question: In deriving C(10, 3) = 10!/(3!·7!), each 3-element set like {3, 6, 7} is the image of how many permutations of the 10 digits?
questions.explanation: The first three entries must be 3, 6, 7 in some order (3! ways) and the last seven are the other digits in any order (7! ways), giving 3!·7! preimages for every set.

questions.question: The recipe 'choose a rank, choose 2 cards of that rank, choose any 3 other cards' is meant to count hands with at least one pair. What is wrong with it?
options: It builds some hands that have no pair
It builds every hand exactly twice, so you must divide by 2
It misses hands with four of a kind
Different hands are built different numbers of times (1, 2, 3 or 6), so it is neither a bijection nor k-to-1
questions.explanation: A hand with one pair is built once, two pairs twice, three of a kind three times, four of a kind six times. Because there is no single k, the division rule cannot fix it.
